Cluster readings (info.kind cluster) should draw nodes only, no edges, and show the name 'no chord name' as today. The four-bar ghost must be a single snapshot to stay calm.

log_to_banter: A 'session card', not a raw dump. The piano page appends the raw MIDI events (on, off, pedal, with a clock-based time t and velocity) plus one DERIVED row at each settled chord change: {t, chord, notes, bass, key, degree, dur, pedalHeldAcrossChange, borrowed}. It batch-POSTs these every 5 s to a new /api/piano/log route in arsenal/serve.py (the same pattern as /api/recordings), which writes state/arsenal/piano-logs/YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.jsonl. When REC starts it writes that time as a marker, so moments line up with the video. On close, a digest runs in node, reusing the THEORY block as-is, and produces a one-page card for the agents. It has four parts. First, his top degree n-grams ('vi-IV-I-V ×14, mostly in Eb'). Second, borrowed chords with timestamps ('bVII at 2:41 and 3:05, from Mixolydian'; 'iv minor at 3:12, borrowed from the parallel minor'). Third, voicing habits: rootless voicings where the name has a root the notes lack, 3-7 shells, left-hand 10ths, extension density. Fourth, pedal habits: the share of chord changes where the pedal was ridden across rather than re-pedalled, and exactly where the wash happened. Every unnamed cluster gets its own entry. The agents open with ONE question aimed at something he does by instinct, anchored to a timestamp he can replay. For example: 'At 3:12 you went from C to Fm6. That minor iv is borrowed from C minor, the classic "bittersweet lift". Did your hand find it, or were you reaching for that sadness?' Unnamed clusters become a game: 'Your hand shape at 1:48 has no name in our templates. Here are three candidate names and why.' The card is stored as an Akashic note so any seat can pick up the thread next session. The raw log stays on disk for anyone who wants to check a claim.

angle: Built for the player. It should read at a glance while your hands are busy. It should draw one rule for what your finger holds and what the pedal holds, show how hard and how together you played, and teach you what your hands just did. I read all 1,691 lines of piano.js, the r4 9:16 receipt, serve.py and take.py. Two findings shape both schemes. (1) The engine already follows CC64. onMidiMessage calls setSustain(d[2] >= 64) and the dim tail is the pedal. What is missing is a clear picture of it, and the raw pedal value, because half-pedalling is cut off at 64. The loop already runs at the monitor's rate through rAF, and only REC is held to 60 fps through requestFrame. (2) Why the screen turns into a wall: the trail shader uses additive blending. Each bar has a halo pad of 1.2 x its width on each side, about 0.77 units for a white key, so neighbouring halos overlap and add up. The core is multiplied by up to 1.9, which pushes a held bar at L 0.76 over the bloom threshold of 0.9. The glow at each bar's foot adds more on top. Both schemes fix this with the same rules: no additive halos, gaps between columns, brightness kept under the bloom threshold except for a short flash on each note-on, and a layout where the notes never pass behind the chord name or the staff. Both also share one rule for pedal notes: SOLID = your finger is holding it, HOLLOW = only the pedal is. The r4 receipt also shows the front edge of the keys at about y 1560, inside the bottom 20% of the frame (1536-1920). Change the lens shift from 0.25 to about 0.21 and take a new receipt to confirm the key fronts end at or above y 1520.

schemes.name: Rehearsal Roll
schemes.pitch: Notes rise up the screen in columns like FL's piano roll turned on its side, with every chord name riding up beside its own notes, so a clip reads like a lead sheet you can watch your hands write.
schemes.visuals:
LAYOUT for 9:16 (1080x1920). y 0-230: empty. y 240-540: chord band. The chord name is left-aligned at x 72, size 150 (same drawLabel, with LAYOUT label {cx 330, cy 380, w 620, h 300, align left}). A small grand staff sits on the right: LAYOUT staff {cx 830, cy 390, w 420, h 320, s 13}. Behind the band, a vertical scrim goes from rgba(1,2,6,0.92) at y 240 to 0 at y 600. y 600-1330: the roll. Set uTop so the fade (the last 15%) ends at screen y 600, so a bar never passes behind text. y 1340-1520: the 3D keyboard, with the lens shift retuned. y 1536-1920: floor and fog only. In 16:9 the roll fades out by y 380, and the label and staff keep the band above it.
COLUMNS: no halo pad. White bars are 0.72 units wide. Black bars are 0.40 wide, at z +0.02, with a 0.05 outline in #010206 so they cut cleanly over the white column next to them. Use normal blending with premultiplied alpha, not additive.
HELD PART (aT0..aT1): solid fill in the existing pitch hue. L = 0.46 + 0.36*v^0.8 (v = vel/127), C 0.14. Linear luminance stays at or under 0.8, so it never blooms.
ONSET CAP: the top edge of the bar, which marks the note-on moment. Its height is 0.10 + 0.22*v units at L 0.92. For the first moments it is multiplied by 1 + 1.2*exp(-age/0.12): a single bloom flash that settles. A loud note gets a thick cap and a pp note a hairline, so dynamics are readable from any still frame.
PEDAL TAIL (aT1..aT2): hollow. A 2 px outline (fwidth-based), alpha 0.7*exp(-tailAge/1.5) with a floor of 0.28, and an interior fill at alpha 0.07. The tail length is exact.
NOTE-ON: the key goes down (existing), the cap flashes, and sparks fire only when v > 0.7, so they mark accents instead of making noise.
NOTE-OFF with no pedal: the bar's bottom edge closes and the glow at its foot turns off within 60 ms.
SUSTAIN PEDAL: (1) A pedal region: one instanced quad across the whole keyboard (x 0, w 58, z TRAIL_Z-0.06), amber oklch(0.80 0.12 68). Its alpha is 0.05*(cc64/127), so a half pedal shows as a fainter band. The edge where the pedal went down is a solid 1.5 px line at alpha 0.45. The edge where it came up is dashed (0.5 units on, 0.3 off; the dashes are fixed in world space and ride with the roll, so they never crawl). (2) The rail line eases from copper to amber oklch(0.85 0.13 70) x1.4. (3) The felt strip rises 0.10 units over 60 ms, like dampers lifting. (4) The staff layer draws the Bravura Ped. glyph (U+E650) under the bass staff while the pedal is down, and the release asterisk (U+E655) for 600 ms after it comes up.
CHORD CHANGE: when overlay.update settles a new chord, draw a 1 px line across the whole roll at the chord's earliest note-on (INK alpha 0.16). Add a chord-name sprite (Archivo 600, about 30 px at span 16) on a dark pill (rgba(1,2,6,0.72), radius 8). The pill sits just above that line, right-aligned to keyX(lowest note) - 0.5, so the name rides up the roll next to its own bass note. If the chord's note-ons spread over 30 ms or more, the caption adds 'rolled 84 ms' with an up or down arrow for the direction, and a 1 px INK 0.35 line joins the onset caps in time order. The overlay's existing pop still fires.
TIMING GRID: only when MIDI clock arrives (0xF8 at 24 ppqn, with 0xFA/0xFC, from FL through loopMIDI). Beat lines at INK 0.06, bar lines at 0.12, a small bar number in the right margin. With no clock, draw no grid: never invent a tempo.
schemes.theory_value: Harmonic rhythm: the spacing between chord lines is how long each chord lasts. Progression history: Fmaj9, G9, Em7, Am9 stack up the screen as a readable chart. Voicing shape: a spread voicing and a close one make different column patterns, and the thick onset cap shows which voice you leaned on. Pedal technique: in good legato (syncopated) pedalling, the pedal comes up at the chord change and goes down again just after the new chord's line. If you lift late, the old chord's hollow tails cross below the new chord's line on top of its solid bars. That is the smear, drawn exactly where you hear it. Chord roll direction and spread in ms show whether a chord was struck together or arpeggiated, and which hand led. With FL clock on, it also shows whether you play ahead of or behind the beat.
schemes.tiktok_value: Producers already read piano rolls, so it lands with FL and Kontakt TikTok at once. The chord names riding up with their notes give a paused or screenshotted frame the whole progression, not just the current chord, and that is what people comment on and stitch. Solid-versus-hollow makes pedal use visible without explanation. Flat, crisp columns with one flash per note-on survive TikTok's re-encode far better than a bloom wall. The chord band stays clear of the platform UI zones.
schemes.sustain_behaviour: Held notes are solid and pedal-only notes are hollow outlines. The outline alpha decays to a floor of 0.28, so a 20 s pedal leaves thin readable lines instead of glow. Columns never overlap (black bars are narrower, in front, with a dark outline). There are no halos and no additive blending, and bars stay under the bloom threshold, so a fully pedalled passage adds up to a set of thin outlines and never a wall. The pedal itself is a separate background band at 5% alpha with crisp edges. The rail and the felt give a mechanical 'pedal is down' cue that keeps flashing out of the notes. The roll fades out before the chord band, so the name and staff stay readable whatever you play.
schemes.build_sketch:
REUSE: keyX/isBlack, noteLch/noteColor (add an L override for velocity), the trail instancing pattern (InstancedBufferGeometry, analytic uNow placement, slot recycling in trails.start/release/end), camera and lens shift, bloom unchanged, keys and noteLights, overlay makeLayer/drawLabel/drawStaff with a new LAYOUT variant per scheme, and Theory.detect.
NEW: (1) A `scheme` select next to #color-select (localStorage arsenal.piano.scheme). (2) The trail shader split into three instanced pools sharing one ShaderMaterial source with defines: pedal regions and grid lines (64 slots, renderOrder 0), white notes (400, renderOrder 1), black notes (240, renderOrder 2). Separate pools make the normal-blend draw order deterministic. Fragment work: SDF fill, a fwidth outline for the hollow tail, the cap band, and a dash pattern for pedal-up edges (about 90 lines of GLSL). (3) Engine: store the raw CC64 value as sustainValue. setSustain opens and closes the pedal-region instance. The threshold for which notes sound stays at 64. (4) Chord markers: a pool of 24 Meshes with 512x96 CanvasTextures, redrawn only when a chord changes. Their y is set on the CPU each frame (24 writes is nothing at 240 Hz). Hook them in overlay.update where `this.shown = this.pending`, using the minimum t0 of that chord's notes from `sounding`. (5) MIDI clock: onMidiMessage currently returns early for 0xF8/0xFA/0xFC; count ticks into a beat phase and emit grid instances. (6) Lens shift 0.25 to 0.21 in 9:16.
SIZE: about 450 lines. RISKS: premultiplied alpha under NeutralToneMapping (check colours against noteCss in a receipt); sprite text passing through bloom (keep luminance under the threshold); the order of overlapping white and black columns; chord markers sliding if the camera zooms out a lot (they are world-anchored, so they shrink rather than slide). ACCEPTANCE RECEIPT: replay a dense pedalled MIDI take from Daniel's own playing, then take a receipt showing the chord band's contrast is intact and no roll pixel is over the bloom threshold outside the onset flashes.

schemes.name: Ring-Out
schemes.pitch: See what is actually still ringing: every note gets a mixer meter that decays like a real string, the pedal lifts a visible damper rail, and the screen tells you whether your melody sings over the chord.
schemes.visuals:
LAYOUT for 9:16. y 0-230: empty. y 240-520: chord label (the existing centred drawLabel, size 160). Its caption line becomes a performance readout, updated only when a chord changes: 'melody +18 · rolled 60 ms ↑'. y 540-640: dynamics strip, a 900x90 px area at x 90-990. It covers the last 10 s, scrolling right to left. Each note-on is a 7 px dot in its note hue at y = 630 - 80*v; top-voice onsets are 10 px INK rings. Faint guide lines sit at v 0.25/0.5/0.75, and a 1 px INK 0.12 tick marks each chord change. y 660-1000: grand staff, LAYOUT staff {cx 540, cy 830, w 860, h 440, s 20}. y 1010-1330: meter field, at most 4.8 world units above the rail, about 320 px. y 1340-1520: keyboard plus damper rail. y 1536+: floor only. Because the meters are short and live only in the present, nothing ever passes behind the label or the staff.
METERS: one instanced quad per sounding note (pool of 128). White bars are 0.70 wide; black bars are 0.42 at z +0.02 with a dark outline. The level is computed in the vertex shader. L0 = v^1.6. While held or pedalled, level = L0*exp(-(min(now,aT2)-aT0)/tau), with tau(m) = 7.0*2^(-(m-21)/24): A0 7 s, A4 1.75 s, C8 0.57 s. After the sound ends (aT2), level *= exp(-(now-aT2)/0.09). Height = 4.8*sqrt(level). Fill is a vertical gradient in the note hue from L 0.40 at the bottom to L 0.78 at the top, kept under the bloom threshold.
HELD notes are solid. PEDAL-ONLY notes are hollow: a 2 px outline at alpha 0.75 and fill at alpha 0.10, the same rule as Rehearsal Roll.
PEAK-HOLD TICK: a 0.07-unit line at the height L0 gave the meter. It holds for 1.0 s, then falls at 5 units/s until it meets the bar. All of this is computed from aT0 in the shader. It is INK for the current top voice and note hue at L 0.9 otherwise.
NOTE-ON: the bar jumps up with a 40 ms rise, and the top gets 1 + 1.0*exp(-age/0.12), the only bloom. The key goes down (existing). A dot lands in the dynamics strip. Striking the same key again closes the old instance and starts a new peak tick, so repeated-note dynamics show.
NOTE-OFF with no pedal: the meter collapses in about 0.3 s. You see the damper land.
SUSTAIN PEDAL: a 3D damper rail, a RoundedBox 52.2 x 0.22 x 0.5 at y RAIL_Y+0.12, z TRAIL_Z+0.25, in front of the meter bases. It is dark felt 0x1a0d10 with a thin front strip (52.2 x 0.035 x 0.035) glowing oklch(0.84 0.13 70). As CC64 goes from 0 to 127, the rail rises by 0.55*(value/127) units (eased, tau 0.03) and the strip's glow goes from 0.15 to 1.3. A half pedal is a half lift. On pedal up, every unheld meter drops together, which is exactly what a pedal lift sounds like. The staff shows the Bravura Ped. glyph while the pedal is down and the release asterisk for 600 ms after.
CHORD CHANGE: the label pops (existing). The balance and spread readout is recomputed. A tick is added to the dynamics strip.
MUD TINT: while the pedal is down, check any two sounding notes below MIDI 52 (E3) that are 1-3 semitones apart and both have level > 0.15. If found, those meters' outlines turn oklch(0.70 0.12 35). This is the low interval limit, made visible. Check at 10 Hz on the CPU and write aWarn only when it changes.
schemes.theory_value: Dynamics as phrasing: the strip shows crescendo and diminuendo arcs across a phrase, so 'I played it flat' becomes visible. Voicing the melody: 'melody +18' versus 'melody buried -4' is the most useful single piano-practice check, and the INK peak tick shows which note counts as the top voice. Register physics: treble meters vanish while bass lingers under the pedal, which is why pedalled bass gets muddy and treble does not. The low interval limit (close intervals below about E3 blur) appears exactly when he plays it. What the pedal physically does (lifts every damper), plus how pedalling is written in a score (Ped. and the release asterisk). The 'rolled 60 ms ↑' and 'together' captions give chord-attack timing.
schemes.tiktok_value: Mixer meters with peak hold are native to producer audiences, and the rising damper rail is a satisfying mechanical beat that lands on every pedal change. It shows only the present, so any clip cut makes sense without context and loops cleanly. The balance caption and the mud tint create commentable teaching moments ('why is my bass orange?'). The frame is sparse and high-contrast, which suits phone screens and re-encoding. There is no history to crowd the staff, which stays large and readable.
schemes.sustain_behaviour: Pedalled notes are hollow and decay by register, so a dense pedalled passage thins from the top down in about 1-2 s. Only the bass lingers, as it does acoustically. There are no history columns, so a wall cannot form: the most on screen is the number of sounding notes, in a pool of 128. Peak ticks fall away after 1 s. Brightness stays under the bloom threshold except for a 120 ms flash on each note-on. The pedal state lives on its own object (the damper rail and the Ped. glyph), not in the notes, so it stays clear even when every note is pedalled. Pedal up is the visible cutoff where all unheld meters drop at once.
schemes.build_sketch:
REUSE: keys, noteLch/noteColor, the instancing and slot logic from trails (the attributes aX, aW, aT0, aT1, aT2, aVel and aColor map one-to-one onto meters), noteOn/noteOff/setSustain as the only producers, bloom, camera, the overlay label and staff layers with a new LAYOUT variant, Bravura (already loaded), and Theory.detect.
NEW: (1) meterMesh: InstancedBufferGeometry plus attributes aTop (is top voice) and aWarn. Vertex shader for the analytic level, peak hold and flash (about 45 GLSL lines); fragment shader for the gradient, hollow outline and tick (about 40). Reclaim a slot when the analytic level < 0.01. (2) Damper rail: 2 meshes plus eased lift from the raw CC64 value (about 30 lines JS). (3) Dynamics strip: THREE.Points in overlayScene, a ring buffer of 256 onsets, its own uNow shader. It is placed in overlay pixel space, so it is crisp and after bloom (about 60 lines). (4) Pure analysis added inside the THEORY block so the node tests cover it: Theory.attack(onsets) returns {spreadMs, direction}, and Theory.balance(onsets) returns {topMidi, topVel, restMean, verdict}, working on the note-on group within 150 ms of the chord's first note-on (about 60 lines). (5) The mud check, using the same tau formula on the CPU (about 30 lines). (6) drawStaff draws the Ped. glyph, and the staffKey adds the pedal state so it redraws only when the pedal changes.
SIZE: about 350 lines. RISKS: (a) tau is a stylised piano model. A Kontakt pad or strings patch sustains forever, so add a 'sustaining patch' toggle (tau = infinity while held, 0.4 s release). (b) Meters can read as a generic graphic EQ unless the damper rail and the solid/hollow rule are clearly visible. (c) The top-voice choice for a melody played after the chord: use the highest note-on within 150 ms of the chord, or a later higher note-on while the chord still sounds. (d) Peak-tick motion must stay in the shader to keep the CPU flat at 144-240 Hz.

log_to_banter: Bookmark from the keys. Log every piano event into the existing take ledger (arsenal/take.py through POST /api/take/open and /api/take/<id>/events). Use the presentation clock that PLAY-NIGHT-SPEC defines, {clock:"presentation", epoch:0, ticks:round(performance.now()), timebase:"1/1000"}, and batch once a second. Events: {kind:"note_on", midi, vel}, {kind:"note_off", midi}, {kind:"cc64", value} (the raw value), and a derived {kind:"chord", name, notes, key, spreadMs, balance} each time the label settles. Add one performer-first event: learn a KeyLab pad (the UI says 'press the pad you want as Bookmark') so Daniel can hit it mid-take without leaving the keys. That writes {kind:"bookmark"} and shows a HUD-only tick, never on the recorded canvas. A new `py -m arsenal takes digest <id>` runs the THEORY block in node, the same way the tests extract it, and turns the 20 s before each bookmark into a compact digest. The digest holds: the chord progression with Roman numerals in the guessed key; how long each chord lasted; voicing facts (top note, spread, inversion, shell or rootless); pedal habits (for example 'pedal-up 240 ms after the chord change'); velocity balance and phrase shape; and progressions he repeats across the session. The agents get only the digest, so it costs little, and they open with a question, not a lecture. For example: 'At bookmark 2 you went Fmaj9 to Fm6. That's the minor iv borrowed from C minor, the bittersweet move. Did you reach for it on purpose, or did your hand find it?' Daniel says what he felt, and the agents name what he did.

angle: This takes Daniel's words at face value: a piano at the bottom, and every note climbs straight up out of its own key, like a piano roll. Both schemes plug into the notes engine as it is. trails.start/release/end become a scheme interface: {start(m,vel,t), release(ref,t), end(ref,t), pedal(on,depth,t), chord(info,tOnset), frame(t,dt), liveCount(t)}. A "scheme" select sits beside colour-select, saved under arsenal.piano.scheme, and the current look stays as "Aurora". piano.js already reacts to CC64: setSustain keeps released notes sounding and draws a dim tail. The bright wall in his playing came from the rendering, not from missing pedal support. It has three causes: AdditiveBlending, a halo pad of 1.2x the bar width on each side (they add up across neighbouring lanes), and bloom picking up the sum, all sitting behind the staff. So both schemes share three rules. (1) Bars use normal alpha blending inside strict lanes with a gutter, so one pixel shows at most one bar and brightness can never exceed a note's own colour. (2) Only held notes and fresh attacks go above luminance 1.0, so bloom grows with how often he strikes keys, not with how many notes the pedal holds. (3) In 9:16 the label and staff move to a top band (y 230-630, next to each other) that the roll never passes behind. The rail sits at y~1290 and the key fronts end by y 1530, so the top 12% and bottom 20% stay free. Scheme 1 is the flat, exact DAW-style roll that reads like FL's piano roll turned upright. Scheme 2 is the cinematic version: blocks slide away down a glass runway, and chord signs recede toward the horizon.

schemes.name: Upright Roll
schemes.pitch: Your playing becomes an FL-style piano roll growing upward out of the real keys. Held notes are solid bars, pedalled ring-out is drawn as a hollow glass outline, and every chord change leaves a labelled hairline, so you can watch your own voicings, rolls and pedal changes scroll past.
schemes.visuals: LAYOUT 9:16 (1080x1920). y 0-230: empty (safe zone). Band y 230-630: the chord label on the left (layer cx 290, w 540, h 400, align left, size starts at 150 and shrinks so the main run is at most 500 px wide, because names like 'Ebm(maj7)/Bb' are long). The pitch-class line sits under it. The grand staff sits on the right at cx 800, cy 430, w 520, h 400, s 15, keeping its elliptical scrim. Roll: y 650-1290. Keys: rail at y~1290, key fronts at or above y 1530 (retune the lens shift from 0.25; elevation 16 deg instead of 22, so lanes read as flat columns). Bias the follow camera so the centroid of recent notes sits at 46% of the width, which keeps the busiest lanes out from under TikTok's right-hand action rail (x > 940). 16:9: label top-left, staff top-right as today, roll across the full width at up to 55% of the height. ROLL PLANE: bars rise along the camera's screen-up vector (uniform uUp = camera.matrixWorld column 1) from the rail point (keyX(m), RAIL_Y, TRAIL_Z). Lanes then stay exactly parallel and aligned with their keys, with no keystoning. Screen speed is a constant 140 px/s: pxPerUnit = framing.w / cam.span, and a CPU odometer scroll += dt*140/pxPerUnit. Each instance stores odometer values (aS0 onset, aS1 release, aS2 end) instead of times, so bars already in flight do not stretch when the camera zooms, and the roll holds about 4.5 s of history. The top 18% of the roll fades out with a smoothstep. LANE GUIDES: a faint 1 px vertical line at every B|C boundary (INK at alpha 0.06) and a slightly darker backdrop behind black-key lanes (alpha 0.03). They are static relative to the keys, so nothing crawls. BARS: SDF rounded rectangles of lane width minus a 3 px gutter (white lane about 0.88 of a key, black about 0.50), anti-aliased with fwidth. NOTE-ON: a bar is born at the rail and grows upward while the key is held. The solid fill uses the note's OKLCH colour at L = 0.62 + 0.22*vel and alpha 0.92, with a narrow emissive core (x1.4, the only part of the bar that blooms). The top 8 px of the bar is an attack cap at L+0.12 that fades from x1.8 to x1.0 over 0.3 s. A rolled chord therefore shows as a visible staircase of caps. At the rail, a 0.25 s horizontal flash 1.6x the lane width replaces most sparks (keep burst() at 25% count; the flash is deterministic, with no random shimmer). NOTE-OFF with the pedal up: the bottom edge leaves the rail, the bar closes into a rounded pill and rises away, and the key springs back as it does now. NOTE-OFF with the pedal down: the solid part stops at the release point and the segment from there to the rail becomes a HOLLOW tube. It has a 2 px border in the same hue at L 0.70, C 0.12, alpha 0.75, and an interior fill whose alpha starts at 0.16 and decays with exp(-age/2.5) toward 0.05, like a piano string dying away. Each note reads as 'held for this long, rang for this long'. SUSTAIN PEDAL: a pedal lane is a 12 px strip pinned 18 px inside the left edge of the frame (world x = cam.x - cam.span/2 + margin, recomputed every frame), rising on the same odometer. It is filled amber (oklch 0.80 0.14 68, alpha 0.55) while CC64 is down and empty while it is up, so every gap marks a pedal change. At the rail end of the strip a SMuFL keyboardPedalPed glyph (U+E650) lights up while the pedal is down and a pedal-up glyph (U+E655) flashes on release. The rail line brightens from 0.9 to 1.5 while the pedal is down. PEDAL LIFT: every hollow tail ends at the same odometer value, which cuts a clean horizontal edge across all lanes: a visible pedal change. CHORD CHANGE: when overlay.shown commits a new name, find tOnset = the earliest t0 among sounding notes with t0 >= overlay.pendingSince - 0.25. Spawn a hairline across the visible width at that odometer value (INK alpha 0.35, 2 px), plus a small tag with the chord name (Archivo 600, 34 px) just above it at the left, next to the pedal lane. The line rides up with the roll. Tags are drawn in the overlay scene after bloom, positioned by camera.project() each frame, and the roll top fades them out. MUD TINT: when a chord commits, any tail that started before that commit and whose pitch class is not played among the new chord's fresh notes eases its chroma from 0.12 to 0.03 over 250 ms. This mixes toward a precomputed same-L, same-hue grey stored in an aColorMud attribute, so the easing is perceptual. Leftover pedal ring then shows as grey glass under the new chord's colours.
schemes.theory_value: The roll shows three things the chord label cannot. (1) Duration and articulation: legato, staccato and overlapping bars are visible, and you can see how long you actually hold chord tones compared with letting the pedal carry them. (2) Voicing geometry: lane spacing makes open and close voicings, left-hand shells (root plus 7th), doubled roots and the top-note melody line easy to see. The attack-cap staircase shows roll order and whether he arpeggiates up or down. (3) Pedal technique, which Daniel does by feel: hollow tails that end a little after the new chord's solid tops mean 'syncopated/legato pedalling done right'. Grey mud tails crossing a chord hairline mean 'you held the pedal through a harmony change', so the blur is visible and he can decide whether he wants it (it is sometimes lovely, e.g. a pedal point). Chord hairlines with names turn the roll into a lead sheet that scrolls past him, so chord symbols and actual notes line up in time, which is exactly the link he says he doesn't fully understand.
schemes.tiktok_value: Viewers get it instantly. A piano roll growing out of real 3D keys is the Synthesia look turned upside down, and every producer has seen FL's piano roll, so it reads as 'this is a producer' in the first second. The solid-versus-hollow contrast gives dense pedalled playing a glassy, layered look instead of a white-out. The attack-cap staircases on rolled chords are satisfying to watch. The chord name stays sharp and readable in the top band for the whole clip, and hairline tags drifting up let a viewer pause and read the progression. Both are good for comments and saves ('what's the chord at 0:07?').
schemes.sustain_behaviour: While a key is held the bar is solid and its core may bloom. After release under the pedal the bar becomes a hollow outline whose interior fades like a decaying string, so pedalled notes stay visible and keep their structure while contributing no bloom and at most 16% fill. Lanes never overlap (3 px gutters and normal blending), so a pedalled cluster of 30 notes turns into a curtain of separate glass tubes at about 15% fill, not a summed white wall. Only notes whose keys are physically down can go above luminance 1.0. Pedal lift cuts all tails along one horizontal line. The amber pedal lane shows CC64 down and up regions directly. Half-pedal: keep the engine threshold (d[2] >= 64) but also store pedalDepth = d[2]/127, and scale tail border alpha by 0.5 + 0.5*depth, so a continuous pedal on the KeyLab shows partial damping. Muddy leftover ring after a chord change turns grey instead of adding brightness. The top band sits outside the roll area altogether, so it can never be washed out.
schemes.build_sketch: REUSES: 88 keys, keyX/isBlack, noteColor/noteLch/oklchToLinear (plus one extra oklch call per note for aColorMud), the notes engine and CC64 handling, the trail InstancedBufferGeometry pattern (same attributes and slot recycling, times replaced by odometer values), the overlay layers and drawLabel/drawStaff (one new LAYOUT entry plus label auto-fit), burst() at reduced count, updateCamera (new elevation, shift and centroid bias per scheme), bloom (retuned: strength 0.3, threshold 1.0, radius 0), and the THEORY block untouched. NEW CODE: (a) scheme registry and select, about 40 lines. (b) Odometer plus rebase: every 10 minutes subtract a constant from every aS* value and from the odometer, to keep Float32 precision; about 20 lines. (c) Trail shader rewrite with the uUp billboard, gutter SDF, hollow-tail branch, attack cap, mud mix and top fade; about 110 lines of GLSL and JS. (d) Pedal lane as a second small instanced mesh (64 slots, attributes aS0/aS1, x taken from uniform uPedalX) plus the pedal glyph in a tiny overlay layer; about 60 lines. (e) Chord hairlines (instanced quads, 24 slots) and name tags (a CanvasTexture per name with an LRU of 16, placed in overlayScene via camera.project); about 90 lines. It needs a hook in overlay.update where shown changes: scheme.chord(shown, tOnset). (f) Lane guides, about 30 lines. (g) A 'pedal storm' demo phrase (four octaves of pedalled arpeggios, 30+ notes under one pedal) plus a CDP receipt frame that asserts the mean luminance of the label and staff band stays within 5% of silence. TOTAL: roughly 380-450 lines. RISKS: odometer desync if a frame is skipped (integrate using the clamped dt, same as today); tags jittering if camera.project runs before updateCamera (run it after); black lanes at full 88-key span are about 12 px wide (fine with fwidth anti-aliasing, but check the receipt at cam.span 57); label auto-fit changes drawLabel metrics used in 16:9 (gate it by layout). Rendering is time/odometer based with no per-frame per-note CPU work, so it is independent of refresh rate at 60, 144 or 240 Hz, and REC's paced 60 fps requestFrame is unaffected.

schemes.name: Progression Runway
schemes.pitch: Each note is a lit glass block that slides away from the keys down a mirrored runway toward the horizon, and every chord change plants a road sign with its name and scale degree (IVmaj9, V9, iii7, vi9), so the last twenty seconds of the progression stretch into the distance like a lead sheet you're flying over.
schemes.visuals: LAYOUT 9:16. Same top band as the Upright Roll (label left, staff right, y 230-630). Camera is the player's view from above and behind the keys: fov 36, elevation 38 deg, lookTarget (cam.x, 1.1, -26), lens shift tuned so the rail projects to y~1300, key fronts end at or above y 1530, and the fog-out point 110 units back projects to y~650, just under the band. Tune by checking camera.project on (cam.x, 1.0, -30) and (cam.x, 1.0, -115) in a receipt. The far, fogged runway therefore sits below the text and never behind it. 16:9: fov 26, horizon at about 40% of the height, label top-left, staff top-right. DECK: a dark glass plane at y 1.0 from z -5.7 (just behind the back rail) to z -170, width 90. MeshPhysicalMaterial colour 0x030409, roughness 0.28, clearcoat 1, the existing envMap, transparent with opacity 0.85 so mirrored blocks show faintly through. A deck shader draws only octave lines (B|C) with fwidth anti-aliasing, alpha 0.07, fading out wherever line spacing drops below 8 px, so perspective creates no moire or crawl. Manual fog in every custom shader: mix toward stageTint using smoothstep(25, 110, viewDepth). BLOCKS (held segment, onset to release): an InstancedBufferGeometry from BoxGeometry(1,1,1) translated so it spans y 0..1 and z 0..-1. The vertex shader sets zNear = TRAIL_Z - (now - min(now,aT1))*5.0 and zFar = TRAIL_Z - (now - aT0)*5.0, height = 0.18 + 0.37*vel, width 0.84 (white) or 0.50 (black), x = keyX. Faces are shaded by normal: top face x1.0 of the note colour, sides x0.55, far face (the onset cap) as emissive x(1 + 1.2*exp(-age/0.3)), which blooms only right after the strike. Blocks are opaque with depthWrite on, so no sorting is needed. MIRROR: the same geometry drawn a second time with y mirrored about the deck, alpha 0.18, fading by exp(-depthBelowDeck*3). RIBBONS (pedal-sustained segment, release to end): a flat plane geometry on the deck (y 1.005) that shares the SAME InstancedBufferAttribute objects as the blocks (one upload), drawing z from aT1 to aT2 (or to now while still sounding). Lane-wide, normal blending, alpha 0.12 + 0.43*exp(-(now - aT1)/2.2), with a brighter outer 12% at each edge (alpha +0.25) so each ribbon reads as a pair of rails. NOTE-ON: the block is born against the rail with its far face flashing, the key goes down, the rail flashes, and burst() fires at 30% count with sparks drifting back over the deck. NOTE-OFF with the pedal up: the block detaches and slides away with no ribbon (aT2 = aT1). NOTE-OFF with the pedal down: the block detaches and a painted ribbon runs from its near face back to the rail for as long as the note sounds, so the note looks like a struck block trailing a light stripe. SUSTAIN PEDAL: an amber shoulder line (oklch 0.80 0.14 68, width 0.22, alpha 0.6) lies on the deck at world x = cam.x - cam.span/2 + 0.6 (a uniform, so it hugs the left of the view), painted over the z ranges where CC64 was down. The rail line brightens to 1.5 while the pedal is down. PEDAL LIFT: every ribbon ends at the same z, cutting a straight edge across the runway. CHORD CHANGE: at z(tOnset), using the same tOnset rule as the Upright Roll, draw a transverse gate line across cam.span+10 world units (0.05 wide, INK alpha 0.3, fogged). At its left end, place a sign: a THREE.Sprite with a 512x160 CanvasTexture holding the chord name (Archivo 800, 96 px, INK) and, under it, the scale degree (Archivo 700, 56 px). The degree is amber when diatonic and pink (oklch 0.72 0.15 350) for borrowed or chromatic roots. The sign stands 1.1 units above the deck at a world x fixed at spawn (cam.x - 0.36*cam.span), with scale about 3.2x1.0. If the previous sign is less than 2.4 units away in z, put the new one at the right end so they don't overlap. Keep a ring of 10 signs in a separate signScene rendered after composer.render and before the overlay (autoClear false, depthTest false, fog applied as alpha), so the text stays sharp and never blooms. Hide a sign once its projected height is under 18 px.
schemes.theory_value: The runway puts the harmony as a whole on screen, not just the current chord. (1) The progression as a sequence with function: the degree numerals show what his hands do by instinct, e.g. the demo reads IVmaj9, V9, iii7, vi9, ii9, V13, Imaj9 (the Royal Road). This needs a new pure THEORY function degreeName(rootPc, suffix, key): Roman numerals relative to keyGuess.tonic, upper case for major, dominant and augmented qualities, lower case for minor and diminished, b/# prefixes for roots outside the major scale (minor keys measured against the tonic, so bVI and bVII come out naturally), and shown only when keyGuess.r >= 0.7. Node-test it next to detect(). (2) Loops and harmonic rhythm: repeating sign sequences show the loop length, and gate spacing shows how long each chord lasts, making rushing, pushed chords and irregular phrase lengths visible. (3) Borrowed colour: a pink bVII or iv among amber diatonic numerals marks exactly the chords that give his music its 'cinematic' feeling, so he learns their names. (4) Pedalling against harmony: clean pedalling means ribbon cuts coincide with gates, and ribbons running across a gate are harmonic blur, shown in space. (5) Register: block lanes show whether the melody climbs while the bass falls (contrary motion) over several bars at once.
schemes.tiktok_value: Depth and a vanishing point make the shot far more cinematic than a flat roll. It reads like a night highway or a synthwave road built out of the song, a proven, very shareable look. Mirrored blocks on glass add a premium product-shot feel. The receding road signs are the hook: a viewer can read the whole progression name by name after hearing it, which invites 'what's this progression?' comments and saves from other producers. The chord signs make the clip useful for teaching without any caption. The horizon stays dark under the text band, so the label and staff stay crisp for the whole clip, even in loud pedalled climaxes.
schemes.sustain_behaviour: Pedalled notes lie flat: while held, a note is a raised block; after release under the pedal it becomes a painted ribbon on the deck, seen at 38 deg, so its screen area shrinks with distance and fog dims it. Lanes never overlap and ribbons use normal blending, so their brightness is capped at alpha 0.55 of the note colour however many notes the pedal holds. Bloom comes only from block onset caps in the first ~0.3 s after each strike, so a dense pedalled passage shows glowing embers at new attacks over a coloured carpet instead of a cyan-white wall. Ribbon alpha decays like a string (time constant 2.2 s, floor 0.12), so a long pedal gradually dims rather than building up. The amber shoulder line shows CC64 down and up spans, and pedal lifts cut every ribbon along one straight line. Half-pedal: pedalDepth = d[2]/127 scales new ribbon alpha by 0.5 + 0.5*depth. The label and staff sit in a band above the fogged horizon, where no bright geometry ever reaches.
schemes.build_sketch: REUSES: 88 keys (unchanged meshes), keyX/isBlack, noteColor/noteLch, the notes engine and CC64 handling, the attribute layout and slot recycling of the trail instancing (aX/aW/aT0/aT1/aT2/aVel/aColor are shared by the block, mirror and ribbon draws), envMap, stageTint for fog, overlay layers plus the top-band LAYOUT entry shared with the Upright Roll, updateCamera follow logic (new fov, elevation, lookTarget and shift per scheme), burst() at reduced count, bloom (threshold 1.0, strength 0.35, radius 0), and the tOnset chord hook in overlay.update. NEW CODE: (a) deck plane plus octave-line and fog shader, about 70 lines. (b) Block, mirror and ribbon instanced meshes sharing attributes, with face-normal shading, cap emission and manual fog; about 170 lines of GLSL and JS. Hide the existing TRAIL_Z vertical trail mesh in this scheme. (c) Gate lines as instanced quads, 24 slots, about 40 lines. (d) Sign sprites: CanvasTexture ring of 10, left/right placement, post-bloom signScene render and projected-size cull; about 100 lines. (e) Pedal shoulder instanced strip, about 45 lines. (f) THEORY degreeName plus node tests (C major: F maj9 -> IVmaj9, Bb -> bVII, E m7 -> iii7; A minor: F -> VI, G -> VII, E7 -> V7), about 60 lines. (g) Camera preset plus receipt checks (runway horizon under the band, pedal-storm luminance in the band), about 40 lines. TOTAL: roughly 520-620 lines. Consider moving both schemes into sibling modules (piano-roll.js, piano-runway.js) that import shared exports from piano.js, since the file is already ~1,690 lines. RISKS: the back rail box (top at y~1.11) can hide the nearest ~1 unit of runway at low elevation, so start the deck at z -5.7 and keep elevation at or above 34 deg; lane-line aliasing in perspective (mitigated by the fwidth fade and octave-only lines); sprites piling up in 9:16 zoomed-in follow (use the side-alternation rule); sign x fixed at spawn drifting off-screen when the camera pans far (acceptable, or clamp x to the view on spawn only); if keyGuess flips mid-song, earlier signs keep their old numerals (by design, a historical record); transparent ribbons against the transparent deck need renderOrder set: mirror, then deck, then ribbons, then blocks. Everything is clock-driven on the GPU, so it runs at 60 Hz or monitor-native rates with identical motion, and REC stays paced at 60.

log_to_banter:
A "What was that?" button with an always-on play log.

**The log.** piano.js keeps a 30-minute ring buffer of raw events: note on/off with velocity, CC64 value, and timestamps from clock(). It also keeps the derived chord timeline: each committed overlay.shown with its tOnset, spelled notes plus octaves, keyGuess name and r, and pedal state. The page writes both as NDJSON to state/arsenal/playlogs/YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.ndjson through a small POST /api/playlog route beside the existing /api/recordings route.

**The button.** Daniel assigns a spare KeyLab 88 mk3 button to CC 20 in Arturia MIDI Control Center, and onMidiMessage handles CC 20. When he plays something he doesn't understand, he taps it. The page then saves a "moment": the last 12 seconds cut from the buffer, compressed into a transcript an LLM reads easily. One line per chord, for example: `+0.00s Fmaj9 (F2 C3 | A3 C4 E4 G4) ped down, key C major, IV` and `+1.43s G9 ...`. It also includes his onset-order voicing (roll direction), pedal changes, and any notes the chord detector could not name.

**The reply.** The moment goes to the claude seat over the bus. An agent answers with a fixed three-part shape:
- **Name it:** "you played IVmaj9, V9, iii7, vi9, the Royal Road".
- **Why it works:** a common-tone or voice-leading explanation grounded in his actual notes, e.g. "your top voice E-F-D-C steps down while the bass climbs".
- **Try this:** one variation to play next, e.g. "swap the iii7 for a III7 (E7) and feel the pull to vi".

**Session digest.** A nightly job mines the full logs for his habits: his most-used chord qualities, favourite borrowed chords (for example a bVII he keeps returning to), loop lengths, and "pedal held through a chord change" counts. These become banter openers in his own vocabulary, like "you reach for maj9 over a 5th-less left hand constantly; that's a Neo-soul shell, want to know why it sounds expensive?" The conversation always starts from something he actually played, not from a textbook.
